newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada proceeding with mission despite Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Canada proceeding with mission despite Zaire.

text.p: Canada said on Thursday it had enough support to push ahead with the initial steps of an international aid mission for eastern Zaire, despite opposition from Zaire's government to a key part of it.

Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said at least 15 countries including the United States had agreed to participate in the first stage, and a "steering board" meeting would be convened on Friday to give final confirmation.

"At that time, we are quite confident that the proposal that we made to move forward, to give us a more active presence of the international force, will be launched," he said, addressing a National Press Club breakfast.

Canada is leading an international effort to get aid to what western officials say is at least 200,000 refugees and perhaps hundreds of thousands more in strife-torn eastern Zaire, in addition to Zairians displaced in their country.
Two parts of the latest Canadian proposal were to set up a military headquarters at Entebbe, Uganda, and to pursue organised reconnaissance to determine how many people needed what.

The third is "to develop the capacity for air delivery of supplies so that where the humanitarian organisations felt there was a need and couldn't reach large numbers of people there would be that air capacity," he said.

It was a carefully chosen set of words that appeared to leave open the possibility of not actually dropping food by air if opposition from aid groups, which prefer truck convoys, and Zaire proved insurmountable.

But Axworthy made two points in response to the declaration by Zairian Information Minister Boguo Makeli that the government was categorically opposed to food drops and that it would not authorise overflights for such purposes.
"I'm not sure he speaks for the government. As you know, things in the country are very confused, and who speaks for what are a question mark," Axworthy said.

He added that in any case the U.N. Security Council's authorisation of an international force to assist in the return of refugees and in the delivery of aid was called under Chapter VII of the U.N. Charter.
That article allows member countries to proceed with air, sea or land operations to maintain or restore international peace and security in carrying out Security Council tasks.
Canada has voiced the frustration of many with the delays in mounting aid to refugees. "There is still an ongoing tragedy," Axworthy said.

The Security Council resolution was on November 15 and no mission has begun operating since, partly because of confusion on the need after the return of around 600,000 refugees to Rwanda and partly because the Rwandan government has refused to allow the force to operate from its territory.

Axworthy reported a breakthrough, however, in that in addition to allowing force commander Canadian Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril to tour eastern Zaire, Rwanda had also allowed non-governmental organisations (NGOs) to go in for 10 days.

"The Rwandan government, in discussions with General Baril, in the last 24 hours has agreed that they would open up for a 10-day period for the NGOs to go into Zaire to do a much closer evaluation as to what the needs are," he said.
Axworthy said the Friday meeting of the steering body, or contact group, would be probably be in New York or Ottawa and would be at the level of officials rather than ministers.
He said some of the 15 countries had agreed to provide troops. Other participation was in the form of planes, staff command, engineering, medical supplies, food and money.
